choices: Defend each sentence the editor questioned
Ask whether each note serves what you meant, then accept what does
check.why: The paragraph is not the ego; a writer weighs each note against the purpose and keeps what helps.

lessons.title: A Style Checklist You Will Use
lessons.mainIdea: A short checklist run on every draft catches most style problems, and a checklist works only if it is short enough to actually run.
reading: Every writer has read lists of a hundred rules and used none of them, because a hundred rules is a book, not a tool. A *checklist* you will actually use fits on an index card and takes ten minutes per page. Here is one built from this unit, in the order that catches the most with the least work. One: is the point in the first sentence of the paragraph, or is it hiding at the end? Two: read only the first few words of each sentence; does the string cohere? Three: circle every word ending in -tion, -ment, -ance, -ity; can it become a verb? Four: cross out every 'very,' 'really,' 'thing,' 'kind of' and 'the fact that'; does the sentence survive?

Five: find every sentence over thirty words and every run of three sentences under eight; break or combine. Six: read the last word of each sentence; is the weight where you want it? Seven: read one paragraph aloud; does it sound like a person or a machine? That is seven checks. Written on a card, it is shorter than this paragraph. Run it on a real draft and you will find the same three or four problems every time, because every writer has habits. After a month, cross off the ones you have stopped making and add the one your editor keeps circling.

The checklist has one rule of its own: run it after the draft, never during. Cutting while you write freezes the writing, because the editor in your head is louder than the writer. Write the bad, long, filler-heavy draft freely. Then put on the editor's hat, take out the card, and cut. Devon's three hundred words were not a failure. They were the draft that had to exist before the hundred and twenty could. The pencil comes second. But it does come.

words.d: a short, fixed list of things to check, run the same way every time
a pattern a writer repeats without noticing, good or bad
an early version of a piece of writing, meant to be revised

look.title: Strunk's Three Words
look.cite: William Strunk Jr., The Elements of Style, 1918 (a section heading)
look.prompt: Strunk's rule is three words long and practices what it preaches. Which items on the seven-point checklist are really this one rule in different clothes, and which are about something else?

check.q: Why does the lesson insist a checklist must be short?
choices: Because long lists are hard to print
Because a list too long to run is never used
Because there are only seven rules of style
Because short lists sound more formal
check.why: A hundred rules is a book, not a tool; a card you actually run beats a rule you admire.

check.q: Which checklist item targets nominalizations?
choices: Reading the last word of each sentence
check.why: Those endings mark verbs frozen into nouns, which the check asks you to free.

check.q: When should you run the checklist?
choices: After the draft is written, not during
Only on a final printed copy
check.why: Editing during drafting freezes the writing; the bad long draft has to exist before the good short one can.

review.q: 'Each and every student' and 'true fact' are examples of what?
review.why: Both say the same thing twice, which is what redundancy means.

review.q: Which revision frees a hidden verb?
choices: The committee will make a decision soon.
A decision will be made by the committee soon.
The committee's decision is coming soon.
review.why: 'Decide' is the action as a verb; the other versions bury it in the noun 'decision.'

review.q: Why is 'exhausted' better than 'very tired' in most sentences?
choices: Because one precise word beats an intensifier plus a general word
review.why: Intensifiers add no real force; the exact word does the work alone.

review.q: A paragraph of six sentences, each five words long and each beginning with its subject, is most likely to feel what?
review.why: Sameness of length and shape makes prose a tick the reader tunes out.

review.q: Which principle makes a paragraph cohere?
choices: Put a transition on every sentence
Begin each sentence with old information and end with new
Begin each sentence with its subject
Keep all sentences the same length
review.why: Old-to-new lets the reader step from a stone they are on to the next one.

review.q: The lesson compares the plain style to a clean window and the ornate style to what?
review.why: Stained glass is meant to be noticed and admired, as ornate prose is.

review.q: An email to a busy reader should do which of these first?
choices: Thank the reader for their time
review.why: Front-loading the point lets the reader decide in one sentence.

review.q: When editing a classmate's draft, why mark problems instead of rewriting them?
choices: So the writer keeps their voice and learns the pattern
Because rewriting is against the rules
Because the classmate will not notice
review.why: A rewritten paragraph teaches nothing; a marked one lets the writer make the choice.
